content: Surveillance of HIV drug resistance among PrEP users diagnosed with HIV is essential to guide the selection of the most effective first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) combinations for these individuals. This surveillance also evaluates potential cross-resistance to antiretroviral drugs used in both PrEP and ART. Such monitoring is particularly important in countries scaling up PrEP programs. Countries conducting HIV drug resistance surveys are encouraged to perform resistance testing in laboratories designated by the World Health Organization (WHO). WHO has also developed a global HIV drug resistance database, which serves as a repository for de-identified individual-level epidemiological data linked to HIV genome sequences. This database supports countries in ensuring the quality of their data and provides standardized interpretations of resistance patterns. Countries are encouraged to utilize this database for managing HIV drug resistance survey data and to promptly interpret and disseminate findings at the national level and to WHO. This enables timely updates to national and global policies, coordinated responses, and advocacy for action on HIV drug resistance prevention and management. Routine monitoring of quality-of-care indicators and early warning indicators (EWIs) of HIV drug resistance is recommended by WHO to assess whether ART programs are delivering services at the quality needed to minimize the emergence of drug resistance. These indicators help identify gaps in service delivery, allowing corrective actions to optimize clinic and program performance. Annual monitoring of EWIs also enables tracking of improvements or declines over time within and between clinics. Standardized definitions and targets for EWIs have evolved as programs mature, and the most updated set of indicators is included in the 2020 WHO consolidated HIV strategic information guidelines. Monitoring should be conducted separately for adults and children, as determinants and responses may differ. WHO recommends integrating EWI monitoring into routine ART program evaluation systems to minimize costs and strengthen existing data collection and reporting processes. In countries where routine monitoring is not fully implemented or reliable, EWIs can be assessed through a random sample of clinics, with data extrapolated to the national level. For patients with confirmed virological failure, the percentage who switch to second-line ART within 90 days is a critical indicator, with a target of 100%. Comprehensive information on HIV drug resistance is available on the WHO website. The guidelines emphasize the importance of integrating HIV programs into broader health systems and ensuring sustainability through national health financing mechanisms. Countries are encouraged to progressively expand the range of services offered and populations covered, while reducing out-of-pocket expenses for users. WHO also provides tools for estimating the costs and impacts of implementing new recommendations, such as the Spectrum suite of models and the OneHealth tool. These tools assist countries in planning, costing, and evaluating HIV interventions. Additionally, the Optima HIV tool supports epidemic projection and resource allocation optimization, helping countries achieve defined objectives, such as minimizing new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths. The guidelines will be regularly updated based on new evidence and country experiences. Dissemination will be supported through electronic and print publications, as well as regional and subregional meetings.
